Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.

## In 60 seconds

Most tachycardias that mapping systems are asked to explain come down to three mechanisms. A **focus** fires faster
than the sinus node and its waves spread outward from one point. **Reentry** is a wave that keeps finding excitable
tissue ahead of it around a circuit, either fixed by anatomy or scar (**macro-reentry**) or formed by the wave itself.
A **rotor** is a spiral wave turning around a **phase singularity**. Whether reentry can last depends on the
**wavelength**, velocity times refractory period, against the length of the circuit. Whether rhythms stay stable
depends on **restitution**: if action potential duration changes faster than the rest interval, beats start to
**alternate** and waves break. Atrial fibrillation mixes these ideas: focal triggers, often in the pulmonary veins,
start it, and short wavelengths and wave breaks sustain it. A map shows which mechanism fits: activation spreading
outward from an earliest point, or activation covering the whole cycle with early meeting late.

## From the field

- **Short wavelengths go with flutter and fibrillation.** In conscious dogs the atrial wavelength was 14–18 cm during
  normal rhythm; flutter was induced below 9.7 cm and fibrillation below 7.8 cm. The wavelength predicted which
  arrhythmia was induced in 75% of cases, better than refractory period (48%) or velocity (38%) alone [@rensma1988].
- **Atrial fibrillation often starts from a focus.** In 45 patients, 65 of 69 ectopic foci that initiated atrial
  fibrillation (94%) were in the pulmonary veins, firing in bursts of 340 per minute [@haissaguerre1998].
- **Reentry needs no anatomical obstacle.** Allessie and colleagues described circus movement in atrial muscle without
  one, the "leading circle" [@allessie1977].
- **Rotor-guided ablation is contested.** One trial reported 82.4% against 44.9% freedom from atrial fibrillation when
  rotors and focal sources were ablated [@narayan2012]; a later two-center series reported 37% freedom from atrial
  fibrillation at 18 months and called for randomized studies [@buch2016].

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** CV conduction velocity (mm/ms = m/s); ERP effective refractory period (ms); $\lambda$
wavelength (mm); $L$ circuit length (mm); CL cycle length (ms); APD action potential duration, DI diastolic interval
(ms); $f$ the restitution function $\text{APD} = f(\text{DI})$; $\tau_{\text{open}}$, $\tau_{\text{close}}$, $h_{\min}$
the m08 model constants; $\mathbf x_0$ the position of a focus; $T$ activation time.

### Wavelength and reentry

A wave leaves refractory tissue behind it for one refractory period, so it occupies a length of tissue:

$$
\lambda = \text{CV}\times\text{ERP}
$$ {#eq-m10-wavelength}

Rensma and colleagues measured both factors in conscious dogs and found the product a better predictor of induced
arrhythmias than either factor alone [@rensma1988]. Drugs that shorten refractoriness or slow conduction shorten the
wavelength. A wave can circulate around a fixed circuit only if the circuit is longer than its wavelength:

$$
\text{CL} = \frac{L}{\text{CV}}, \qquad L > \lambda, \qquad \text{gap} = L - \lambda = \text{CV}\,(\text{CL} - \text{ERP})
$$ {#eq-m10-circuit}

The **excitable gap** is the stretch of recovered tissue ahead of the front; pacing that reaches it can enter the
circuit, which is what entrainment uses (m11). In a Mitchell–Schaeffer ring whose pulse leaves 75 mm of tissue above
$v_{\text{gate}}$, reentry continued on rings of 90 mm and more and failed on 80 mm; on shorter rings the front ran
into less-recovered tissue and slowed, from 0.31 m/s on a 200-mm ring to 0.25 m/s on a 90-mm ring (lab part B).

::: {.demo #m10-d2 badge="exact"}

```{=html}
<script type="module" src="../demos/m10-d2-circuit.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m10-wavelength and @eq-m10-circuit for a single circuit with uniform velocity and refractory period.
  Tested against `epml.arrhythmia`.
- Parameters: circuit length, velocity and refractory period are free choices for illustration.
- What it ignores: velocity and refractory period that change with the rest interval (lab part B), curvature,
  anatomy and heterogeneity.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- The wavelength $\text{CV}\times\text{ERP}$ is the tissue a wave occupies; a circuit must be longer than it.
- The excitable gap is the circuit's spare room, in millimeters or milliseconds.

### Restitution and alternans

When pacing at cycle length CL, each beat's APD depends on the rest before it, and that rest is what the previous beat
left:

$$
\text{APD}_{n+1} = f(\text{CL} - \text{APD}_n), \qquad \delta_{n+1} = -f'(\text{DI}^*)\,\delta_n
$$ {#eq-m10-restitution}

A small disturbance $\delta$ around the steady state changes sign every beat and grows when the restitution slope
$f'$ exceeds 1: APDs alternate long and short. Nolasco and Dahlen studied this graphically with the restitution curve
and the pacing line [@nolasco1968]. With the m08 closed form, the slope reaches 1 at

$$
\text{DI}_c = \tau_{\text{open}}\ln\!\Big[(1 - h_{\min})\Big(1 + \frac{\tau_{\text{close}}}{\tau_{\text{open}}}\Big)\Big]
$$ {#eq-m10-alternans}

that is DI = 54.7 ms, APD = 95.8 ms and CL = 150.5 ms with the m08 parameters. A paced model cell alternates at a
longer cycle length, 210 ms, and drops to 2:1 capture at 190 ms, because its APDs run longer than the closed form
(lab part C). In guinea pig hearts, repolarization alternated out of phase between neighboring sites above a critical
rate, and a small further acceleration produced unidirectional block, reentry and ventricular fibrillation
[@pastore1999].

::: {.demo #m10-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m10-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m10-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m10-d1-alternans.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the restitution map @eq-m10-restitution with the m08 closed-form restitution ([eq-m08-apd](m08-action-potentials.qmd#eq-m08-apd)), starting 5 ms
  away from the steady state. Tested against `epml.arrhythmia`.
- Parameters: Mitchell–Schaeffer constants as in m08 [@nietoramos2023]; the cycle length is adjustable.
- What it ignores: memory beyond one beat, calcium-driven alternans, coupling to neighboring cells, and the gap between
  the closed form and simulated APDs (m08).
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Restitution slope above 1 makes the steady rhythm unstable: alternans.
- The threshold depends on the whole restitution curve, not on one APD value.

### Rotors and phase singularities

A wavefront that breaks, on an obstacle or on a refractory island, curls at its free end into a spiral. The spiral
turns around a point where all phases meet, a **phase singularity**, and the topological charge of m29
([eq-m29-charge](m29-complex-maps.qmd#eq-m29-charge)) is $\pm1$ around it, the sign giving the direction of rotation
[@bray2001]. In a Barkley-model sheet (illustrative, dimensionless) started with cross-field conditions, one
singularity with charge $-1$ forms at the center; the mirror image has charge $+1$ (lab part D). The spiral's tissue
footprint is set by the same wavelength as above, so short wavelengths allow more rotors in a chamber.

**Key takeaways**

- A rotor is reentry around a phase singularity, with no anatomical obstacle needed [@allessie1977].
- Singularities carry charge $\pm1$; they appear and vanish in pairs.

### Focal or reentrant activation

From a focus at $\mathbf x_0$, activation spreads outward:

$$
T(\mathbf x) = T_0 + \frac{\lvert\mathbf x - \mathbf x_0\rvert}{\text{CV}}, \qquad \text{span} = \frac{\max T - \min T}{\text{CL}} < 1
$$ {#eq-m10-focal}

The activation map has one earliest point and covers only the time to reach the farthest point: 11% of a 300-ms cycle
for a focus in a 40 × 40 mm area at 1.0 m/s. Around a circuit the activation is continuous and covers the whole cycle,
so the latest site borders the earliest ("early meets late") (lab part E). The span depends on how much of the
chamber is mapped, so a partial map of a circuit can look focal. A consensus statement classifies atrial flutter and
regular atrial tachycardia by such mechanisms and their anatomical bases [@saoudi2001].

**Key takeaways**

- Focal: centrifugal spread from an earliest point; the activation span is short.
- Reentry: activation covers the cycle; the map must include the whole circuit to show it.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Mapping is a search for mechanism. Focal sources show centrifugal activation; in one
series most foci that initiated atrial fibrillation were inside the pulmonary veins, 2 to 4 cm from the ostium, with
local activity preceding the ectopic beat on the surface ECG by 106 ± 24 ms [@haissaguerre1998]. Macro-reentry is
classified by its circuit and anatomical basis [@saoudi2001], and its activation covers the cycle (@eq-m10-focal). Whether rotors sustain human atrial
fibrillation is contested: a trial of rotor-guided ablation reported higher freedom from atrial fibrillation
[@narayan2012], and a later series reported poor long-term efficacy [@buch2016]. Wavelength ties these mechanisms to
tissue properties [@rensma1988], and electrical remodeling (m08) shortens it [@wijffels1995].

**What the evidence is.** Animal studies [@allessie1977; @rensma1988; @wijffels1995], a clinical mapping series
[@haissaguerre1998], an isolated-heart study [@pastore1999], a consensus classification [@saoudi2001], a controlled
clinical study [@narayan2012] and a retrospective multicenter series [@buch2016].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Does the map cover the whole circuit?** A partial map of reentry can look focal (@eq-m10-focal).
- **How were singularities detected, with what electrode spacing?** See m29.
- **Was outcome assessed against a control group, with what monitoring?** As the rotor studies show, mechanism
  claims and outcomes need separate evidence.

## How experts think

When a map shows a tachycardia, ask:

1. **Where is the earliest activation, and does activation cover the cycle?** Focal or reentrant (@eq-m10-focal).
2. **If reentrant, where is the circuit, and is it longer than the wavelength?** (@eq-m10-circuit)
3. **Is there an excitable gap?** It decides whether pacing can enter the circuit (m11).
4. **Is the rhythm stable from beat to beat?** Alternation points to steep restitution (@eq-m10-restitution).
5. **For rotors: how were they detected, and would the detector find them in noise?** (m29)

One sentence to keep: **wavelength sets what can fit, restitution sets what stays stable, and the map has to cover
enough of the chamber to tell.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Wavelength (@eq-m10-wavelength) | $\lambda = \text{CV}\times\text{ERP}$ |
| Circuit (@eq-m10-circuit) | $\text{CL} = L/\text{CV}$; needs $L > \lambda$; gap $= L - \lambda$ |
| Restitution map (@eq-m10-restitution) | $\delta_{n+1} = -f'\delta_n$; alternans when $f' > 1$ |
| Alternans onset, closed form (@eq-m10-alternans) | $\text{DI}_c = \tau_{\text{open}}\ln[(1 - h_{\min})(1 + \tau_{\text{close}}/\tau_{\text{open}})]$ |
| Focal spread (@eq-m10-focal) | $T = T_0 + \lvert\mathbf x - \mathbf x_0\rvert/\text{CV}$; span below 1 |
| Rotor ([eq-m29-charge](m29-complex-maps.qmd#eq-m29-charge)) | charge $\pm1$ around a phase singularity |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Dog atrial wavelength 14–18 cm; flutter below 9.7 cm, fibrillation below 7.8 cm; 75% prediction | @rensma1988 |
| 94% of initiating foci in the pulmonary veins; bursts of 340 per minute; 106 ± 24 ms lead | @haissaguerre1998 |
| Rotor-guided ablation 82.4% vs 44.9% freedom from atrial fibrillation | @narayan2012 |
| 37% freedom from atrial fibrillation at 18 ± 7 months | @buch2016 |
| Ring lengths, velocities, alternans thresholds, singularities, spans | our own code |

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. Define the wavelength of excitation and why it matters.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\text{CV}\times\text{ERP}$, the length of tissue a wave keeps refractory. A circuit must be longer than it for
reentry; short wavelengths let more and smaller reentrant waves fit (@eq-m10-wavelength) [@rensma1988].

</details>

**Q2. A drug slows conduction and prolongs refractoriness. What happens to the wavelength?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It depends on the balance; the product can stay the same. Rensma and colleagues saw drugs with opposite effects on
the two factors change the wavelength little [@rensma1988].

</details>

**Q3. What is the excitable gap, and why does an EP study care?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The recovered tissue ahead of the front, $L - \lambda$ or $\text{CL} - \text{ERP}$; pacing captures into the
circuit through it, which entrainment uses (@eq-m10-circuit; m11).

</details>

**Q4. Why can't reentry continue on a ring shorter than the wavelength?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The front reaches tissue still refractory from the same wave and blocks. Near the limit it also slows, because it
travels into less recovered tissue (lab part B).

</details>

**Q5. Explain alternans with the restitution map.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\text{APD}_{n+1} = f(\text{CL} - \text{APD}_n)$; deviations are multiplied by $-f'$ each beat, so with slope above
1 they alternate and grow (@eq-m10-restitution) [@nolasco1968].

</details>

**Q6. Why might alternans lead to fibrillation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

When repolarization alternates out of phase in neighboring regions, steep gradients of refractoriness can block a
wave in one direction and start reentry, as shown in guinea pig hearts (@eq-m10-restitution) [@pastore1999].

</details>

**Q7. What is a phase singularity?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A point around which phase takes every value, so the phase winds by $\pm 2\pi$ around it; a spiral wave turns
around one ([eq-m29-charge](m29-complex-maps.qmd#eq-m29-charge)) [@bray2001].

</details>

**Q8. Does reentry need an anatomical obstacle?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

No: functional reentry, the leading circle or a rotor, turns around tissue kept refractory by the wave itself
[@allessie1977].

</details>

**Q9. How do you tell focal from reentrant activation on a map?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Focal: one earliest site with outward spread and a short activation span. Reentry: activation covering the cycle,
early meeting late. Check that the map covers the circuit (@eq-m10-focal).

</details>

**Q10. Where do atrial fibrillation triggers usually come from?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In the series that showed it, 94% of initiating foci were inside the pulmonary veins [@haissaguerre1998].

</details>

**Q11. A vendor claims rotor maps guide atrial fibrillation ablation. What evidence would you want?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

How rotors were detected and validated, and randomized outcome data with careful monitoring; results so far conflict
[@narayan2012; @buch2016].

</details>

**Q12. Why does electrical remodeling make atrial fibrillation more likely to persist?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It shortens refractoriness, which shortens the wavelength, so more reentrant waves
fit (@eq-m10-wavelength) [@wijffels1995; @rensma1988].

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. CV 0.6 m/s, ERP 150 ms. Wavelength?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

90 mm (@eq-m10-wavelength).

</details>

**S2. A 150-mm circuit conducting at 0.5 m/s. Cycle length?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

300 ms (@eq-m10-circuit).

</details>

**S3. Same circuit, ERP 200 ms. Excitable gap in ms and mm?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

100 ms and 50 mm (@eq-m10-circuit).

</details>

**S4. Restitution slope 0.5 at the steady state. A 4-ms disturbance after two beats?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1 ms, with the same sign as at the start (@eq-m10-restitution).

</details>

**S5. Total charge around a loop enclosing two rotors of opposite rotation?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Zero ([eq-m29-charge](m29-complex-maps.qmd#eq-m29-charge)).

</details>

**S6. A focus in the middle of a 60-mm region at 1 m/s, CL 400 ms. Activation span?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 30 mm / 1 m/s = 30 ms to the edge (more to the corners): under 15% of the cycle (@eq-m10-focal).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Wavelength and arrhythmia type.** Rensma and colleagues plot wavelength for rapid responses, flutter and
  fibrillation [@rensma1988]. This module: wavelength and reentry.
- **Pulmonary vein foci.** Haïssaguerre and colleagues map the sites of initiating ectopic beats [@haissaguerre1998].
  This module: clinical correlate.
- **Rotor maps.** Narayan and colleagues show phase maps of rotors in human atrial fibrillation [@narayan2012]. This
  module: rotors and phase singularities.

## Further reading

- **Reentry.** Leading circle [@allessie1977]; wavelength [@rensma1988]; classification [@saoudi2001].
- **Stability.** Alternans [@nolasco1968; @pastore1999]; phase singularities [@bray2001].
- **Atrial fibrillation.** Triggers [@haissaguerre1998]; remodeling [@wijffels1995]; rotor-guided ablation
  [@narayan2012; @buch2016].
- **Models.** Barkley's two-variable model [@barkley1991]; the cell model of m08 [@nietoramos2023].
- **Related modules.** m08 (action potentials), m09 (propagation), m11 (the EP study), m24 (activation maps), m29
  (complex maps), m41 (locating arrhythmia origins).
